title: La dislocation et les constructions clivées / Dislocation and cleft constructions
bridge: In Spanish, to emphasize an element, word order or intonation is often used (e.g., 'Eso lo vi yo'). In French, dislocation (separating an element with a pronoun and a comma) and cleft constructions (such as 'c'est... qui/que') are much more common and form part of natural syntax, even in formal registers. Note that French does not allow the free word order of Spanish without marking: in French, the subject is usually obligatory, and the emphasized element is placed at the beginning or end with a repetition pronoun.
rule: French cleft constructions (C1) include: 1) 'C'est + X + qui/que + reste de la phrase' to emphasize a subject or object (e.g., 'C'est Marie qui a gagné' — It's Marie who won). 2) Left dislocation ('X, pronom + verbe') or right dislocation ('pronom + verbe, X') to emphasize or clarify the referent (e.g., 'Le prof, il est sympa' or 'Il est sympa, le prof'). In formal registers, right dislocation is more marked and used sparingly. Unlike Spanish, the subject pronoun cannot be omitted in French; dislocation always includes a pronoun. Note that 'c'est' does not agree in number with the emphasized element when used in cleft constructions (e.g., 'C'est eux qui...' not 'Ce sont eux qui...' in formal registers, though 'ce sont' can be found in formal written contexts). For direct or indirect objects, 'que' or 'à qui' (among others) is used.

concept_examples.text: C'est Marie qui a préparé le dîner.
concept_examples.translation: It's Marie who prepared dinner.
concept_examples.phonetic: /s‿ɛ ma.ʁi ki a pʁe.pa.ʁe lə di.ne/

concept_examples.text: Le prof, il est vraiment exigeant.
concept_examples.translation: The teacher, he's really demanding.
concept_examples.phonetic: /lə pʁɔf, il ɛ vʁɛ.mɑ̃ ɛɡ.zi.ʒɑ̃/

concept_examples.text: Ce que je déteste, c'est l'hypocrisie.
concept_examples.translation: What I hate is hypocrisy.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sə kə ʒə de.tɛst, s‿ɛ l‿i.pɔ.kʁi.zi/

concept_examples.text: Il est incroyable, ce film.
concept_examples.translation: It's incredible, this movie.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛ.t‿ɛ̃.kʁwa.jabl, sə film/

common_error.wrong: C'est les enfants qui ont fait les devoirs.
common_error.correct: Ce sont les enfants qui ont fait les devoirs.
common_error.correct_alt: C'est les enfants qui ont fait les devoirs.
common_error.explanation: In formal French, after 'c'est' followed by a plural noun, 'ce sont' is used instead of 'c'est' when the emphasized element is plural. However, in colloquial spoken French, 'c'est' + plural is tolerated. Spanish speakers tend to always use 'c'est' because in Spanish there is no agreement of the copula verb with the attribute in this structure ('Es los niños...' is not said), but in French agreement is mandatory in formal language. Remember: in dislocation, the pronoun that duplicates the dislocated element is obligatory; do not say 'Le prof est sympa' if you want to emphasize 'the teacher,' because it is not dislocation but an unmarked sentence.

examples.original: Moi, je ne suis pas d'accord.
examples.phonetic: /mwa, ʒə nə sɥi pa d‿akɔʁ/
examples.translation: Me, I don't agree.
examples.note: The emphasized element is placed at the beginning and repeated with a pronoun (here 'je'). It is very common in spoken French.

examples.original: Cette idée, elle est géniale.
examples.phonetic: /sɛt i.de, ɛ.l‿ɛ ʒe.njal/
examples.translation: This idea, it's great.
examples.note: Use 'elle' to refer back to the feminine noun. In Spanish, the pronoun is often omitted, but in French it is obligatory.

examples.original: Les vacances, on en parle demain.
examples.phonetic: /le va.kɑ̃s, ɔ̃ ɑ̃ paʁl də.mɛ̃/
examples.translation: Vacations, we'll talk about them tomorrow.
examples.note: The adverbial pronoun 'en' is used to refer back to 'de + les vacances.' Note the agreement.

examples.original: Toi, tu devrais te taire.
examples.phonetic: /twa, ty də.vʁɛ tə tɛʁ/
examples.translation: You, you should be quiet.
examples.note: Left dislocation with a stressed personal pronoun ('toi') followed by the subject pronoun ('tu') is typical for contrast.

examples.original: Elle est très belle, ta maison.
examples.phonetic: /ɛ.l‿ɛ tʁɛ bɛl, ta mɛ.zɔ̃/
examples.translation: It's very beautiful, your house.
examples.note: The emphasized element is placed at the end, after the pronoun. In Spanish, it is more natural to say it at the beginning or without dislocation.

examples.original: Je le connais bien, ce quartier.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə lə kɔ.nɛ bjɛ̃, sə kaʁ.tje/
examples.translation: I know it well, this neighborhood.
examples.note: The pronoun 'le' refers to the direct object that appears later. Useful for adding information afterward.

examples.original: Il faut qu'on y aille, à la plage.
examples.phonetic: /il fo k‿ɔ̃ n‿i aj, a la plaʒ/
examples.translation: We have to go, to the beach.
examples.note: The pronoun 'y' is used to refer back to the place complement. Right dislocation clarifies the referent.

examples.original: C'est bien fait, ton gâteau.
examples.phonetic: /s‿ɛ bjɛ̃ fɛ, tɔ̃ ɡa.to/
examples.translation: It's well done, your cake.
examples.note: Sometimes right dislocation is combined with 'c'est' to give a judgment. In Spanish, we would say 'Está bien hecho tu pastel' without a particle.

levels.label: Les constructions clivées en c'est... qui/que

examples.original: C'est Paul qui m'a prêté ce livre.
examples.phonetic: /s‿ɛ pɔl ki m‿a pʁɛ.te sə livʁ/
examples.translation: It's Paul who lent me this book.
examples.note: Use 'qui' when the emphasized element is the subject. In Spanish, we also use 'quien'.

examples.original: C'est ce que je voulais dire.
examples.phonetic: /s‿ɛ sə kə ʒə vu.lɛ diʁ/
examples.translation: That's what I wanted to say.
examples.note: The cleft construction with 'ce que' (what) is very common for emphasizing an object or idea.

examples.original: C'est à toi que je parle.
examples.phonetic: /s‿ɛ.t‿a twa kə ʒə paʁl/
examples.translation: It's to you that I'm speaking.
examples.note: When the emphasized element is a complement with a preposition, 'que' is used instead of 'qui.' Note the preposition before.

examples.original: Ce n'est pas Marie qui a cassé le vase.
examples.phonetic: /sə n‿ɛ pa ma.ʁi ki a ka.se lə vaz/
examples.translation: It's not Marie who broke the vase.
examples.note: To negate, place 'ne... pas' around 'est.' The cleft construction allows negating a specific element.

title: Registres de langue : soutenu, courant, familier / Language Registers: Formal, Standard, and Informal
bridge: Spanish also uses different registers, but in French the differences are more pronounced and affect not just vocabulary but also syntax and specific constructions. For example, the negation with 'ne' is often omitted in informal speech, which doesn’t happen systematically in Spanish. Additionally, the pronoun 'on' in colloquial French replaces 'nous', whereas in Spanish we always use 'nosotros' across all registers. Be careful with subject-verb inversion in formal questions: in Spanish it’s more flexible and we can use intonation, but in formal French it’s mandatory in certain contexts.
rule: In French, registers are classified into three main levels: soutenu (formal), courant (standard/neutral), and familier (informal). Each register shows lexical variations (e.g., 'voiture' vs 'bagnole'), morphological variations (e.g., negation with 'ne' in formal speech, often omitted in informal), and syntactic variations (e.g., in questions: inversion in formal, 'est-ce que' in standard, intonation or 'tu' in informal). At the C1 level, it’s essential to master the soutenu register for academic and professional contexts and know when to use it appropriately. You should also be familiar with idiomatic expressions and their equivalents in each register. Examples of verbs: 'se rendre' (formal) vs 'aller' (standard) vs 'se tirer' (informal). In writing, the soutenu register is more common; in conversation, courant and familier predominate.

concept_examples.text: Je vous prie de bien vouloir agréer mes salutations distinguées.
concept_examples.translation: I kindly request that you accept my distinguished greetings.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə vu pʁi də bjɛ̃ vu lwaʁ aɡʁe me salytasjɔ̃ distɛ̃ɡe/

concept_examples.text: Vous pouvez me passer le dossier, s'il vous plaît ?
concept_examples.translation: Could you pass me the file, please?
concept_examples.phonetic: /vu puve mə pase lə dosje sil vu plɛ/

concept_examples.text: Tu peux me filer le truc ?
concept_examples.translation: Can you pass me the thing? (colloquial)
concept_examples.phonetic: /ty pø mə file lə tʁyk/

common_error.wrong: Je suis désolé, je ne peux pas venir à la réunion. (in a formal context, not the best example; better: 'Je suis vachement content de vous rencontrer.' in a formal context)
common_error.correct: Je suis ravi de faire votre connaissance.
common_error.correct_alt: Je suis enchanté de vous rencontrer.
common_error.explanation: A typical error is using an overly informal register in formal situations, such as with superiors or in official letters. Words like 'vachement', 'super', or 'truc' are inappropriate in the soutenu register. To avoid this, you should learn formal synonyms and practice switching between registers. In Spanish, formal registers also exist, but the distance between registers isn’t as great as in French, which is why Spanish speakers tend to underestimate the required formality.

examples.original: Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes salutations respectueuses.
examples.phonetic: /vœjəz aɡʁe madam lɛkspʁɛsjɔ̃ də me salytasjɔ̃ ʁɛspɛktɥøz/
examples.translation: Please accept, Madam, the expression of my respectful greetings.
examples.note: A typical courtesy formula in formal letters. Note the subjunctive 'veuillez' (from 'vouloir') and the impersonal structure.

examples.original: Je vous saurais gré de bien vouloir examiner cette affaire.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vu soʁɛ ɡʁe də bjɛ̃ vu lwaʁ ɛɡzamine sɛt afɛʁ/
examples.translation: I would be grateful if you could examine this matter.
examples.note: Use of the conditional to express politeness. 'Sauriez' is the conditional of 'savoir' in this fixed phrase.

examples.original: Il conviendrait de différer notre décision jusqu'à nouvel ordre.
examples.phonetic: /il kɔ̃vjɛ̃dʁə də difeʁe nɔtʁ desizjɔ̃ ʒysk a nuvɛl ɔʁdʁ/
examples.translation: It would be advisable to defer our decision until further notice.
examples.note: Use of the conditional to tactfully suggest. 'Convenir' is formal.

examples.original: Est-ce que vous pouvez m'aider à porter ces cartons ?
examples.phonetic: /ɛs kə vu puve mɛde a pɔʁte se kaʁtɔ̃/
examples.translation: Can you help me carry these boxes?
examples.note: Use of 'est-ce que' to form questions, typical of the standard register.

examples.original: On doit se dépêcher si on veut arriver à l'heure.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ dwa sə depeʃe si ɔ̃ vø aʁive a lœʁ/
examples.translation: We need to hurry if we want to arrive on time.
examples.note: Use of 'on' instead of 'nous' in standard spoken French. In Spanish, there’s no direct equivalent, but it can be translated as 'nosotros'.

examples.original: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vudʁɛ œ̃ kafe sil vu plɛ/
examples.translation: I would like a coffee, please.
examples.note: Conditional of politeness, very common in service situations.

examples.original: On se tire ? J'en ai marre de ce bled.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ sə tiʁ ʒɑ̃nɛ maʁ də sə blɛd/
examples.translation: Shall we leave? I’m fed up with this place.
examples.note: Verb 'se tirer' (to leave), expression 'en avoir marre' (to be fed up), and 'bled' (a remote place, colloquial).

examples.original: T'as vu le nouveau prof ? Il est trop sympa !
examples.phonetic: /ta vy lə nuvo pʁɔf il ɛ tʁo sɛ̃pa/
examples.translation: Have you seen the new teacher? He’s really nice!
examples.note: Omission of 'ne' in negation, 't'as' for 'tu as', apocope 'prof', and use of 'trop' as a positive intensifier.

examples.original: J'ai la flemme de sortir ce soir.
examples.phonetic: /ʒɛ la flɛm də sɔʁtiʁ sə swaʁ/
examples.translation: I can’t be bothered to go out tonight.
examples.note: Idiomatic expression 'avoir la flemme' (to not feel like doing something). No direct equivalent in Spanish.

translations.en: Language Registers: Formal, Standard, and Informal

title: Inversion et antéposition avancées / Advanced inversion and fronting
bridge: In Spanish, interrogative inversion is optional and often avoided ('¿Cuándo vendrás?'), while in French, inversion is mandatory in formal register ('Quand viendrez-vous?'). Additionally, fronting with inversion—such as in 'Peut-être viendra-t-il'—is a much more productive stylistic resource in French than in Spanish, where intonation or fronting without inversion is preferred ('Quizá venga'). For Spanish speakers, the main challenge is remembering subject-verb agreement and the use of the reinforcing pronoun '-t-' in inversion cases where the subject begins with a vowel.
rule: French inversion at the C1 level includes: (1) Simple interrogative inversion (pronoun subject + verb, with hyphen: 'Où vas-tu?') and with nominal subject (subject + verb + repetition pronoun: 'Pierre vient-il?'); (2) Inversion after certain adverbs or phrases like 'peut-être', 'sans doute', 'à peine', 'aussi', 'en vain', which requires inversion in formal/literary register ('À peine a-t-il fini qu'il est parti'); (3) Fronting of complements without inversion (for emphasis) or with inversion in stylistic structures ('Grande est sa surprise'). Exceptions: the adverbs 'peut-être' and 'sans doute' allow variation in informal register, but at the C1 level the canonical form is expected. Note: with 'à peine', tense agreement is used (often 'ne ... que'). In inversions with pronominal subject, elision is not allowed (always 'a-t-il', never 'a-t'il').

concept_examples.text: Où sont mes clés ?
concept_examples.translation: Where are my keys? (interrogative inversion with nominal subject)
concept_examples.phonetic: /u sɔ̃ me kle/

concept_examples.text: Peut-être viendra-t-il demain.
concept_examples.translation: Perhaps he will come tomorrow. (fronting with inversion and reinforcing '-t-')
concept_examples.phonetic: /pøt‿ɛtʁ vjɛ̃dʁa til dəmɛ̃/

concept_examples.text: À peine avait-il commencé qu'il s'est arrêté.
concept_examples.translation: Hardly had he begun when he stopped.
concept_examples.phonetic: /a pɛn avɛtil kɔmɑ̃se kil sɛt aʁete/

common_error.explanation: The error stems from a literal translation of the Spanish 'Quizá él vendrá', where inversion is not mandatory. In French, when 'peut-être' begins a sentence, inversion is required in formal register. In informal register, it can be omitted ('Peut-être qu'il viendra'), but combining 'peut-être' with a subject without inversion or 'que' is incorrect. To avoid this, remember: if 'peut-être' is at the beginning, invert or use 'que'. Neutral alternative: place 'peut-être' after the verb.

examples.original: Où vas-tu ?
examples.phonetic: /u va ty/
examples.translation: Where are you going?
examples.note: Inversion with pronoun subject: verb + hyphen + pronoun. In Spanish, inversion is not necessary.

examples.original: Pierre vient-il ?
examples.phonetic: /pjɛʁ vjɛ̃ til/
examples.translation: Is Pierre coming?
examples.note: With nominal subject, the subject is repeated as a pronoun and inversion is made with that pronoun. In Spanish: '¿Viene Pedro?' without repetition.

examples.original: Peut-être faudrait-il réessayer.
examples.phonetic: /pøt‿ɛtʁ fodʁɛtil ʁeesɛje/
examples.translation: Perhaps we should try again.
examples.note: 'Peut-être' at the beginning requires inversion in formal register. Note the absence of 'que' in the correct construction.

examples.original: Sans doute a-t-elle raison.
examples.phonetic: /sɑ̃ dut a tɛl ʁɛzɔ̃/
examples.translation: No doubt she is right.
examples.note: Here 'sans doute' means 'no doubt' (certainty) and requires inversion. Spanish has no equivalent structure.

examples.original: Grande est sa générosité.
examples.phonetic: /ɡʁɑ̃d‿ɛ sa ʒeneʁozite/
examples.translation: Great is his generosity.
examples.note: Fronting of the attributive adjective in literary style. In Spanish it is possible but uncommon in everyday speech.

examples.original: Aussi ai-je décidé de partir.
examples.phonetic: /osi ɛʒ deside də paʁtiʁ/
examples.translation: So I have decided to leave.
examples.note: 'Aussi' with the meaning of consequence ('so') triggers inversion, unlike its comparative use ('also').

title: Nominalisation complexe / Complex nominalization (process → processing)
bridge: In Spanish, we often use infinitives or constructions with 'el que' to express processes, while French, in formal and academic registers, tends to use nouns derived from verbs (suffixes -tion, -ment, -age, -ure). This allows for more compact and elegant sentences, but requires mastery of morphological derivation and spelling changes. Be careful with false friends (e.g., 'procédure' is not always 'procedura' in all contexts).
rule: In C1 French, complex nominalization is the process of transforming a verb or adjective into an abstract noun to express an action, process, or result. The most common suffixes are: -tion/-sion (transformer → transformation, admettre → admission), -ment (changer → changement, accomplir → accomplissement), -age (nettoyer → nettoyage, abattre → abattage), -ure (couvrir → couverture, ouvrir → ouverture), -ance/-ence (paraître → apparence, dépendre → dépendance). For verbs ending in -ir, -issement is often used (grandir → grandissement, embellir → embellissement). There are spelling changes: ner→ration (coopérer → coopération), ger→tion (naviguer → navigation), yer→iement (nettoyer → nettoyage, but payer → paiement). In academic writing, nominalization allows chaining complements with 'de' (la transformation de l'énergie solaire en électricité). It is widely used in scientific, political, and technical language. Beware: some verbs have two nominalizations with different nuances (presser → pression 'physical/political pressure' vs. pressage 'technical pressing'). For C1, it is essential to choose the correct suffix and avoid calques from Spanish (e.g., do not say 'la processus' but 'le processus'; 'la procédure' is feminine).

concept_examples.text: La transformation numérique des entreprises est un enjeu majeur.
concept_examples.translation: The digital transformation of companies is a major challenge.
concept_examples.phonetic: [la tʁɑ̃sfɔʁmasjɔ̃ nymeʁik de.z‿ɑ̃tʁəpʁiz ɛ.t‿ɛ̃ ɑ̃ʒø maʒœʁ]

concept_examples.text: Le vieillissement de la population affecte l'économie mondiale.
concept_examples.translation: The aging of the population affects the global economy.
concept_examples.phonetic: [lə vjɛjismɑ̃ də la pɔpylasjɔ̃ afɛkt lekɔnɔmi mɔ̃djal]

concept_examples.text: La mise en œuvre de ce plan nécessite une coordination étroite.
concept_examples.translation: The implementation of this plan requires close coordination.
concept_examples.phonetic: [la miz ɑ̃ œvʁ də sə plɑ̃ nesɛsit yn kɔɔʁdinasjɔ̃ etʁwat]

concept_examples.text: L'embauche de nouveaux talents dépend de notre budget.
concept_examples.translation: The hiring of new talent depends on our budget.
concept_examples.phonetic: [lɑ̃boʃ də nuvo talɑ̃ depɑ̃ də nɔtʁ bydʒɛ]

common_error.wrong: La création d'emplois est nécessaire pour améliorer la vie des gens.
common_error.correct: La création d'emplois est nécessaire pour améliorer la vie des citoyens.
common_error.correct_alt: La création d'emplois est nécessaire à l'amélioration de la vie des citoyens.
common_error.explanation: Although the original sentence is not incorrect, 'gens' is too colloquial for a C1 register; 'citoyens' or 'individus' is preferred. Additionally, in academic French, it is common to nominalize the second verb 'améliorer' → 'amélioration' to maintain a consistent nominal structure. The typical error is using verbs instead of nouns in formal contexts, mimicking Spanish structures. To avoid this, always look for nominalization when the text is formal.

examples.original: La décision du gouvernement a surpris tout le monde.
examples.phonetic: [la desizjɔ̃ dy ɡuvɛʁnəmɑ̃ a syʁpʁi tu lə mɔ̃d]
examples.translation: The government's decision surprised everyone.
examples.note: Décision comes from 'décider' (change from -er to -sion). In Spanish, 'decisión' is a cognate, but be careful with spelling.

examples.original: L'industrialisation rapide a transformé le paysage.
examples.phonetic: [lɛ̃dystʁijalizasjɔ̃ ʁapid a tʁɑ̃sfɔʁme lə peizaʒ]
examples.translation: Rapid industrialization transformed the landscape.
examples.note: Industrialisation: suffix -ation based on the verb 'industrialiser'. Note that in Spanish it is 'industrialización', with a 'z'.

examples.original: La communication non verbale est essentielle en réunion.
examples.phonetic: [la kɔmynikasjɔ̃ nɔ̃ vɛʁbal ɛ.t‿esɑ̃sjɛl ɑ̃ ʁeynjɔ̃]
examples.translation: Non-verbal communication is essential in a meeting.
examples.note: Communication: -tion, but in Spanish 'comunicación'. Watch out for the 'm' (not 'n').

examples.original: Le déplacement des travailleurs quotidiens est un problème majeur.
examples.phonetic: [lə deplasmɑ̃ de tʁavajœʁ kɔtidjɛ̃ ɛ.t‿ɛ̃ pʁɔblɛm maʒœʁ]
examples.translation: The daily commute of workers is a major problem.
examples.note: Déplacement: -ment from 'déplacer'. In Spanish, 'desplazamiento' has the same root, but the suffix differs.

examples.original: Le nettoyage du site a pris plus de temps que prévu.
examples.phonetic: [lə nɛtwajaʒ dy sit a pʁi ply də tɑ̃ kə pʁevy]
examples.translation: The cleaning of the site took longer than expected.
examples.note: Nettoyage: -age, but 'nettoyer' changes the 'y' to 'i' before -age. In Spanish, 'limpieza' is a distinct noun.

examples.original: L'embouteillage sur l'autoroute a causé des retards.
examples.phonetic: [lɑ̃butɛjaʒ syʁ lotoʁut a koze de ʁətaʁ]
examples.translation: The traffic jam on the highway caused delays.
examples.note: Embouteillage: -age with double 'l'. Do not confuse with 'bouteille' (bottle).

examples.original: La poursuite de ses études l'a conduit à l'étranger.
examples.phonetic: [la puʁsɥit də se.z‿etyd lɑ kɔ̃dɥi a letʁɑ̃ʒe]
examples.translation: The continuation of his studies led him abroad.
examples.note: Poursuite comes from 'poursuivre' (irregular, not 'poursuivage'). It is a special case.

examples.original: La saisie des données doit être faite avant la réunion.
examples.phonetic: [la sezi de dɔne dwa ɛtʁ fɛt avɑ̃ la ʁeynjɔ̃]
examples.translation: The data entry must be done before the meeting.
examples.note: Saisie: from the verb 'saisir', does not follow common patterns. In Spanish, 'captura' or 'introducción'.

examples.original: L'accroissement des inégalités préoccupe les économistes.
examples.phonetic: [lakʁwasmɑ̃ de.z‿ineɡalite pʁeɔkyp le.z‿ekɔnɔmist]
examples.translation: The increase in inequalities concerns economists.
examples.note: Accroissement: from 'accroître', with 'ss' and 'ement'. Be careful with the double 's'.

title: L'ellipse et la substitution / Ellipsis and substitution
bridge: In Spanish, to avoid repetitions we use constructions like 'yo también', 'yo tampoco', 'a mí también' or 'a mí tampoco' with conjugated verbs. In French, however, pronouns 'aussi' and 'non plus' are used, but the most characteristic forms are 'si' and 'non' after verbs like 'croire', 'penser' or 'espérer', along with substitution by pronouns 'le', 'la', 'les' and 'en'. The big difference is that in French the neutral pronoun 'le' is often used to refer back to a complete idea, something that in Spanish is resolved with 'lo' but less frequently, and it can lead to confusion because in French 'le' can refer to a masculine noun or to an entire proposition. Additionally, in short answers 'oui' and 'non' are often replaced by 'si' and 'non' after verbs of opinion, which has no direct equivalent in Spanish.
rule: Ellipsis (omission of repeated elements) and substitution (replacement with pro-forms) are essential in French to avoid redundancies. For short answers: 'Oui, je pense' → 'Je pense que oui' / 'Je ne pense pas' → 'Je pense que non'. 'Si' is used to contradict a negative: 'Tu n'aimes pas ça ? – Si, j'aime ça.' To express agreement: 'Moi aussi' (affirmative), 'Moi non plus' (negative), although in careful register 'Aussi moi' or 'Non plus moi' are used (less common). To substitute a noun phrase: 'le/la/les' according to gender and number, respecting the agreement of the past participle if present: 'Tu as vu mes clés ? – Je les ai vues.' To substitute a complement with 'de': 'en' is used. To substitute an attribute or an already mentioned infinitive: 'Je le suis' (with 'être'), 'Je le veux' (with 'vouloir'). To substitute a place with 'à': 'y' is used. Regarding ellipsis, in comparative and coordinated structures common elements are omitted: 'Pierre aime le vin, et Marie le fromage' (omits 'aime'). The verb is also elided in short answers with 'oui/non/si'. Exceptions: 'le' is not used with verbs like 'être' in certain contexts; 'l''être' can be used. In the case of 'en' and 'y', they are not used with people (except in fixed expressions); tonic pronouns are used. For C1 level, it is important to master substitution in subjunctive and conditional, and ellipsis in complex sentences with 'que'.

concept_examples.text: Je pense que oui, mais je ne suis pas sûr.
concept_examples.translation: I think so, but I'm not sure.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə pɑ̃s kə wi mɛ ʒə nə sɥi pa syʁ/

concept_examples.text: Tu as fini tes devoirs ? – Oui, je les ai finis.
concept_examples.translation: Did you finish your homework? – Yes, I finished them.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ty a fini te dəvwaʁ wi ʒə le ɛ fini/

concept_examples.text: Elle aime le café, et moi aussi.
concept_examples.translation: She likes coffee, and I do too.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɛm lə kafe e mwa osi/

concept_examples.text: Tu n'es pas venu ? – Si, je suis venu hier.
concept_examples.translation: You didn't come? – Yes, I came yesterday.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ty nɛ pa vəny si ʒə sɥi vəny jɛʁ/

common_error.wrong: Je suis d'accord aussi, mais je ne le pense pas.
common_error.correct: Je suis d'accord, mais je ne le pense pas.
common_error.correct_alt: Je suis d'accord, mais je ne pense pas.
common_error.explanation: The error comes from translating literally 'yo también estoy de acuerdo, pero no lo pienso'. In French, 'aussi' is not used with 'd'accord' in that position; it would be 'moi aussi' at the beginning, or simply 'je suis d'accord'. Additionally, 'je ne le pense pas' is correct ('le' substitutes an idea), but adding 'aussi' creates redundancy. Another option would be 'je suis d'accord, mais je ne pense pas ça' (less formal). The key is that in French, substitution with 'le' already covers the idea, and 'aussi' is reserved for expressing agreement with a previous statement.

levels.label: Les réponses courtes : si, non, que oui, que non
levels.translation: Short answers: yes, no, that yes, that no

examples.original: Tu viens ? – Oui, je viens.
examples.phonetic: /ty vjɛ̃ wi ʒə vjɛ̃/
examples.translation: Are you coming? – Yes, I am.
examples.note: Basic use of 'oui' to affirmatively answer a question without negation.

examples.original: Tu ne viens pas ? – Si, je viens !
examples.phonetic: /ty nə vjɛ̃ pa si ʒə vjɛ̃/
examples.translation: Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!
examples.note: 'Si' is used to contradict a negative in the question. It does not always correspond to 'sí' in Spanish; it is specific to French.

examples.original: Je pense que oui, mais je ne suis pas certain.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə pɑ̃s kə wi mɛ ʒə nə sɥi pa sɛʁtɛ̃/
examples.translation: I think so, but I'm not sure.
examples.note: In subordinate clauses with verbs of opinion, 'que oui' / 'que non' is used to summarize a proposition.

examples.original: Elle espère que non, car elle préfère rester.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɛspɛʁ kə nɔ̃ kaʁ ɛl pʁefɛʁ ʁɛste/
examples.translation: She hopes not, because she prefers to stay.
examples.note: The same structure with 'espérer' and other verbs of thought.

levels.label: L'accord et le désaccord : aussi, non plus, moi si
levels.translation: Agreement and disagreement: also, neither, I do

examples.original: J'aime le jazz. – Moi aussi !
examples.phonetic: /ʒɛm lə dʒaz mwa osi/
examples.translation: I like jazz. – Me too!
examples.note: To show agreement with a positive statement, 'moi aussi' is used. In Spanish we say 'yo también', but here the subject pronoun is not translated literally; instead, the tonic pronoun is used.

examples.original: Je ne fume pas. – Moi non plus !
examples.phonetic: /ʒə nə fym pa mwa nɔ̃ plys/
examples.translation: I don't smoke. – Me neither!
examples.note: To agree with a negative, 'non plus' is used. Be careful: do not confuse it with 'aussi', which only goes with affirmations.

examples.original: Tu n'aimes pas le fromage ? – Si, j'adore ça !
examples.phonetic: /ty nɛm pa lə fʁɔmaʒ si ʒadɔʁ sa/
examples.translation: You don't like cheese? – Yes, I love it!
examples.note: 'Si' is also used in short answers to contradict a negative, just like in level 1, but here it is used to express disagreement with the other person's negation.

examples.original: Elle n'est pas partie, et moi non plus.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl nɛ pa paʁti e mwa nɔ̃ plys/
examples.translation: She didn't leave, and neither did I.
examples.note: 'Moi non plus' can be used as a tonic subject to emphasize; in Spanish we would say 'yo tampoco'.

levels.label: La substitution pronominale : le, en, y

examples.original: Es-tu fatigué ? – Oui, je le suis.
examples.phonetic: /ɛty fatige wi ʒə lə sɥi/
examples.translation: Are you tired? – Yes, I am.
examples.note: 'Le' substitutes an attributive adjective. In Spanish we use 'lo', but in French it is invariable in this case and does not agree.

examples.original: Tu as des questions ? – Oui, j'en ai deux.
examples.phonetic: /ty a de kɛstjɔ̃ wi ʒɑ̃n e dø/
examples.translation: Do you have any questions? – Yes, I have two.
examples.note: 'En' substitutes a complement with 'de' (des questions). In Spanish it is omitted or 'de ellas' is used, but in French it is mandatory.

examples.original: Ils vont à Paris ? – Ils y vont demain.
examples.phonetic: /il vɔ̃ a paʁi il i vɔ̃ dəmɛ̃/
examples.translation: Are they going to Paris? – They are going tomorrow.
examples.note: 'Y' substitutes a place complement with 'à'. It is placed before the conjugated verb, just like the other pronouns.

examples.original: Cette idée, je la trouve excellente.
examples.phonetic: /sɛt ide ʒə la tʁuv ɛksɛlɑ̃t/
examples.translation: This idea, I find it excellent.
examples.note: Here 'la' substitutes 'cette idée' (feminine singular) and agrees. In Spanish we also use 'la', but be careful with the order and redundancy.

title: Marqueurs discursifs avancés / Advanced discourse markers for cohesion
bridge: In Spanish, we use connectors like 'no obstante', 'por consiguiente' or 'a saber' to organize discourse. In French, there are similar markers, but with different nuances and collocations. For example, 'en effet' does not always mean 'en efecto' (sometimes it means 'because'), and 'certes' is more formal than 'ciertamente'. Be careful with word order and register: some markers are exclusively formal or written.
rule: Advanced discourse markers in French are classified by their function: opposition (cependant, néanmoins, en revanche), cause (en effet, car, étant donné que), consequence (par conséquent, de ce fait, ainsi), reformulation (autrement dit, en d'autres termes, c'est-à-dire), concession (certes... mais, bien que, quoique) and discourse organization (d'abord, ensuite, enfin, en somme). At C1 level, precise and varied use is expected, avoiding repetitions. Pay attention to punctuation: many of these markers are used between commas or at the beginning of a sentence. In French, 'en effet' is used to confirm something previously stated, unlike the Spanish 'en efecto', which often has a more emphatic use.

concept_examples.text: Les résultats sont encourageants ; en effet, le taux de réussite a augmenté de 10 %.
concept_examples.translation: Los resultados son alentadores; en efecto, la tasa de éxito ha aumentado un 10%.
concept_examples.phonetic: /le ʁezylta sɔ̃t‿ɑ̃kuʁaʒɑ̃ ; ɑ̃n‿efɛ, lə ʁo də ʁɥesi a oɡmɑ̃te də dis puʁsɑ̃/

concept_examples.text: Il est très compétent. Néanmoins, son manque d'expérience se fait sentir.
concept_examples.translation: Es muy competente. No obstante, su falta de experiencia se nota.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛ tʁe kɔ̃petɑ̃. neɑ̃mwɛ̃, sɔ̃ mɑ̃k d‿ɛkspeʁjɑ̃s sə fɛ sɑ̃tiʁ/

concept_examples.text: Nous devons agir rapidement ; autrement dit, il n'y a pas de temps à perdre.
concept_examples.translation: Debemos actuar rápidamente; en otras palabras, no hay tiempo que perder.
concept_examples.phonetic: /nu dəvɔ̃ aʒiʁ ʁapidəmɑ̃ ; otʁəmɑ̃ di, il n‿j a pa də tɑ̃ a pɛʁd/

concept_examples.text: Certes, le projet est ambitieux, mais il est réalisable.
concept_examples.translation: Ciertamente, el proyecto es ambicioso, pero es realizable.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sɛʁt, lə pʁɔʒɛ ɛt‿ɑ̃bisjø, mɛ il ɛ ʁealizabl/

common_error.wrong: Il a plu toute la journée, en effet je suis resté chez moi.
common_error.correct: Il a plu toute la journée ; par conséquent, je suis resté chez moi.
common_error.correct_alt: Comme il a plu toute la journée, je suis resté chez moi.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'en efecto' can be used to indicate a consequence, but in French 'en effet' only introduces a justification or clarification of what was said. To express consequence, use 'par conséquent', 'donc' or 'de ce fait'. Avoid literal translations and think about the logical function.

examples.original: Ce produit est cher ; cependant, il est de très bonne qualité.
examples.phonetic: /sə pʁɔdy ɛ ʃɛʁ ; səpɑ̃dɑ̃, il ɛ də tʁɛ bɔn kalite/
examples.translation: Este producto es caro; sin embargo, es de muy buena calidad.
examples.note: 'Cependant' is equivalent to 'sin embargo', but in French it can appear after the semicolon or at the beginning of the clause. Here it is at the start of the second clause after the semicolon.

examples.original: Je ne suis pas d'accord avec toi. En revanche, je respecte ton opinion.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə nə sɥi pa d‿akɔʁ avɛk twa. ɑ̃ ʁəvɑ̃ʃ, ʒə ʁɛspɛkt tɔ̃ ɔpinjɔ̃/
examples.translation: No estoy de acuerdo contigo. En cambio, respeto tu opinión.
examples.note: In this context, 'en revanche' introduces a soft contrast, similar to 'en cambio' in Spanish.

examples.original: Il aurait pu réussir ; or, il n'a pas travaillé.
examples.phonetic: /il ɔʁe py ʁeysiʁ ; ɔʁ, il n‿a pa tʁavaje/
examples.translation: Habría podido tener éxito; sin embargo, no trabajó.
examples.note: 'Or' is a logical opposition marker widely used in formal argumentation; it does not mean 'o'.

levels.label: Marqueurs de cause et de conséquence
levels.translation: Discourse markers of cause and consequence

examples.original: Le trafic est dense ; par conséquent, nous arriverons en retard.
examples.phonetic: /lə tʁafik ɛ dɑ̃s ; paʁ kɔ̃sekɑ̃, nu aʁivʁɔ̃ ɑ̃ ʁətaʁ/
examples.translation: El tráfico está denso; por consiguiente, llegaremos tarde.
examples.note: 'Par conséquent' is formal; in conversation 'donc' is more commonly used.

examples.original: Étant donné les circonstances, nous avons reporté la réunion.
examples.phonetic: /etɑ̃ done le siʁkɔ̃stɑ̃s, nu avɔ̃ ʁəpɔʁte la ʁeynjɔ̃/
examples.translation: Dadas las circunstancias, hemos pospuesto la reunión.
examples.note: 'Étant donné' requires a noun or pronoun; it is not conjugated. Pay attention to agreement.

examples.original: Elle a réussi son examen grâce à son travail acharné.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a ʁeysi sɔ̃n‿ɛgzamɛ̃ ɡʁas a sɔ̃ tʁavaj aʃaʁne/
examples.translation: Ella aprobó su examen gracias a su trabajo incansable.
examples.note: 'Grâce à' introduces a positive cause; for negative causes, use 'à cause de'.

examples.original: Nous avons dû annuler le vol ; en effet, la tempête était forte.
examples.phonetic: /nu avɔ̃ dy anyle lə vɔl ; ɑ̃n‿efɛ, la tɑ̃pɛt etɛ fɔʁt/
examples.translation: Tuvimos que cancelar el vuelo; en efecto, la tormenta era fuerte.
examples.note: Here 'en effet' justifies the cancellation, it does not express a consequence.

levels.label: Marqueurs de reformulation et de concession
levels.translation: Discourse markers of reformulation and concession

examples.original: Le problème est complexe ; autrement dit, il nécessite une analyse approfondie.
examples.phonetic: /lə pʁɔblɛm ɛ kɔ̃plɛks ; otʁəmɑ̃ di, il nesesit yn‿analiz apʁɔfɔ̃di/
examples.translation: El problema es complejo; en otras palabras, requiere un análisis profundo.
examples.note: 'Autrement dit' is widely used to reformulate an idea; in Spanish, 'en otras palabras'.

examples.original: Il a accepté l'offre, en d'autres termes, il est prêt à déménager.
examples.phonetic: /il a aksepte l‿ɔfʁ, ɑ̃ dotʁ tɛʁm, il ɛ pʁɛ a demenaʒe/
examples.translation: Aceptó la oferta, en otros términos, está listo para mudarse.
examples.note: More formal variant of 'autrement dit'.

examples.original: Bien que le coût soit élevé, l'investissement en vaut la peine.
examples.phonetic: /bjɛ̃ kə lə ku swa elve, lɛ̃vɛstismɑ̃ ɑ̃ vo la pɛn/
examples.translation: Aunque el costo sea alto, la inversión vale la pena.
examples.note: 'Bien que' is followed by the subjunctive; a common error is to use the indicative, influenced by Spanish.

examples.original: Certes, les résultats sont satisfaisants, mais ils restent perfectibles.
examples.phonetic: /sɛʁt, le ʁezylta sɔ̃ satisfəzɑ̃, mɛ il ʁɛst pɛʁfɛktibl/
examples.translation: Ciertamente, los resultados son satisfactorios, pero siguen siendo mejorables.
examples.note: The structure 'certes... mais' is typical of formal concession.

title: Atténuation et modalisation fine / Attenuation and fine nuance
bridge: In Spanish, to soften statements we use the subjunctive, conditionals, and adverbs like 'quizás' or 'posiblemente'. In French, in addition to these strategies, the conditional of politeness and impersonal structures such as 'il semblerait que' or 'il est possible que' are frequently used, which require the subjunctive. A common pitfall: the Spanish 'parece que' is constructed with the indicative, but in French 'il semble que' can take either the indicative or subjunctive depending on the nuance (certainty vs. doubt).
rule: To express distancing and nuance in French at the C1 level, the following are used: 1) The passé and present conditional with verbs like 'pouvoir', 'devoir', 'vouloir' to suggest hypotheses or politeness (e.g., 'Il aurait pu venir' – He could have come). 2) Impersonal structures followed by the subjunctive: 'il est possible que', 'il semble que' (when expressing doubt), 'il est peu probable que'. 3) Modal adverbs: 'peut-être', 'sans doute', 'apparemment', 'vraisemblablement' which require inversion or the subjunctive in elevated registers. 4) The 'conditionnel de reportage' for unconfirmed information (e.g., 'Le président aurait signé' – The president is said to have signed). 5) Attenuation periphrases: 'j'aurais tendance à penser', 'je dirais que', 'pour ainsi dire', 'en quelque sorte'. Key rules: the subjunctive is used after expressions of doubt/possibility, but 'il me semble que' with certainty takes the indicative; 'peut-être que' in colloquial register uses the indicative, but in formal register it inverts: 'Peut-être est-il…'.

concept_examples.text: Il semblerait que le projet soit déjà terminé.
concept_examples.translation: Parecería que el proyecto ya está terminado.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il sɑ̃.bʁə.ʁɛ kə lə pʁɔ.ʒɛ swa de.ʒa tɛʁ.mi.ne/

concept_examples.text: J'aurais tendance à penser qu'il vaut mieux attendre.
concept_examples.translation: Yo tendería a pensar que es mejor esperar.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿o.ʁɛ tɑ̃.dɑ̃s a pɑ̃.se k‿il vo mjø a.tɑ̃dʁ/

concept_examples.text: Peut-être serait-il plus sage de reporter la réunion.
concept_examples.translation: Quizás sería más prudente posponer la reunión.
concept_examples.phonetic: /pø.t‿ɛt sə.ʁe.t‿il ply saʒ də ʁə.pɔʁ.te la ʁe.y.njɔ̃/

concept_examples.text: Le directeur aurait accepté la proposition, selon certaines sources.
concept_examples.translation: El director habría aceptado la propuesta, según ciertas fuentes.
concept_examples.phonetic: /lə di.ʁɛk.tœʁ o.ʁe ak.sɛp.te la pʁɔ.po.zi.sjɔ̃ sə.lɔ̃ sɛʁ.tɛn suʁs/

common_error.wrong: Il semble que le problème est résolu.
common_error.correct: Il semble que le problème soit résolu.
common_error.correct_alt: Il me semble que le problème est résolu.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish 'parece que' is constructed with the indicative ('Parece que el problema está resuelto'). In French, 'il semble que' in the sense of doubt or attenuation requires the subjunctive; only when expressing certainty ('il me semble que') is the indicative used. To avoid this error, identify whether the statement expresses certainty or doubt: if it expresses doubt, use the subjunctive.

examples.original: Je voudrais vous demander un conseil.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vu.dʁɛ vu də.mɑ̃-de œ̃ kɔ̃.sɛj/
examples.translation: Querría pedirle un consejo.
examples.note: The conditional of politeness softens the request; in Spanish we would also use the conditional ('querría') or 'quisiera'.

examples.original: Tu pourrais m'aider à préparer cette présentation ?
examples.phonetic: /ty pu.ʁɛ m‿ɛ-de a pʁe.pa.ʁe sɛt pʁe.zɑ̃.ta.sjɔ̃/
examples.translation: ¿Podrías ayudarme a preparar esta presentación?
examples.note: The conditional 'pourrais' is more polite than 'peux'. In Spanish, the conditional is used similarly, but sometimes the imperfect of politeness ('¿podías?') is used, which is uncommon in French.

examples.original: Il aurait pu prendre un autre train.
examples.phonetic: /il o.ʁe py pʁɑ̃dʁ œ̃ o.tʁə tʁɛ̃/
examples.translation: Él podría haber tomado otro tren.
examples.note: The past conditional (aurait pu) expresses an unrealized hypothesis about the past, equivalent to the compound conditional in Spanish.

examples.original: Il est possible qu'elle vienne demain.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛ pɔ.sibl k‿ɛl vjɛn də.mɛ̃/
examples.translation: Es posible que ella venga mañana.
examples.note: After 'il est possible que', the subjunctive is used, just as in Spanish ('es posible que venga').

examples.original: Il semble que les négociations soient au point mort.
examples.phonetic: /il sɑ̃bl kə le ne.ɡɔ.sja.sjɔ̃ swa o pwɛ̃ mɔʁ/
examples.translation: Parece que las negociaciones están estancadas.
examples.note: When 'il semble que' expresses doubt, the subjunctive is used; however, 'il me semble que' takes the indicative because it implies a personal judgment.

examples.original: Il est peu probable que nous ayons le temps.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛ pø pʁɔ.babl kə nu.z‿ɛ.jɔ̃ lə tɑ̃/
examples.translation: Es poco probable que tengamos tiempo.
examples.note: Note that 'il est peu probable que' requires the subjunctive, just as in Spanish.

examples.original: Peut-être devrions-nous revoir notre stratégie.
examples.phonetic: /pø.t‿ɛt də.vʁi.jɔ̃ nu ʁə.vwaʁ nɔtʁ stʁa.te.ʒi/
examples.translation: Quizás deberíamos revisar nuestra estrategia.
examples.note: In formal register, 'peut-être' triggers inversion of the subject and verb. In Spanish, no such inversion is required.

examples.original: Apparemment, il n'y a plus aucun espoir.
examples.phonetic: /a.pa.ʁa.mɑ̃ il n‿j a ply o.kœ̃ ɛs.pwaʁ/
examples.translation: Aparentemente, ya no hay ninguna esperanza.
examples.note: 'Apparemment' allows the statement to be softened, similar to 'al parecer' in Spanish.

examples.original: Pour ainsi dire, ce projet est un échec.
examples.phonetic: /pu.ʁ‿ɛ̃.si diʁ sə pʁɔ.ʒɛ ɛ.t‿œ̃.n‿e.ʃɛk/
examples.translation: Por así decirlo, este proyecto es un fracaso.
examples.note: This expression is useful for softening a blunt statement, equivalent to 'por así decirlo' in Spanish.

title: Patrones verbales complejos / Complex Verb Patterns
bridge: In Spanish, direct and indirect object pronouns can often be combined with relative freedom (e.g., 'se lo di' vs. 'le lo di' is incorrect), but in French, the order of unstressed pronouns is more rigid and varies depending on the verb mood (affirmative, imperative, negation). Additionally, in French, there is agreement of the past participle with the direct object when it precedes the verb, a phenomenon that does not occur in Spanish. Another key contrast is that French verbs like 'penser' or 'croire' require different structures (often with 'à' + infinitive or 'que' + subjunctive) that in Spanish are more direct with infinitive or indicative.
rule: In French, direct object pronouns (me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les) and indirect object pronouns (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur) are placed before the verb in most tenses, following the pattern: subject + (ne) + pronoun(s) + verb (in compound tenses: auxiliary + past participle). The order of pronouns is: 1st direct object (me/te/se/nous/vous) and 2nd indirect object (lui/leur), except in affirmative imperative where they come after the verb and 'moi/toi/lui' is used for the indirect object. In negation, pronouns precede the verb. When there are two pronouns, the direct object comes before the indirect one, except with 'lui' and 'leur' pronouns, which always come after the direct object (e.g., 'le lui', 'la leur'). In affirmative imperative, the order reverses: verb + direct object pronoun + indirect object pronoun, with hyphens. The past participle agrees when the direct object (CD) precedes the verb in compound tenses: 'Je les ai vus' (I saw them) vs. 'Je leur ai parlé' (I spoke to them). Typical uses include verbs that govern 'à' (parler à, téléphoner à, demander à) and verbs that govern 'de' (avoir besoin de, se souvenir de, se méfier de). At C1 level, mastering the combination of pronouns in structures like 'se le', 'le lui', 'me le', etc., and the difference with Spanish (where 'se' is used to avoid cacophony) is essential.

concept_examples.text: Je le lui ai donné.
concept_examples.translation: I gave it to him/her.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə lə lɥi e dɔne/

concept_examples.text: Elle me l'a expliqué.
concept_examples.translation: She explained it to me.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl mə l‿a ɛksplike/

concept_examples.text: Donne-le-lui !
concept_examples.translation: Give it to him/her!
concept_examples.phonetic: /dɔn lə lɥi/

concept_examples.text: J'y pense souvent.
concept_examples.translation: I often think about it.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿i pɑ̃s suvɑ̃/

common_error.wrong: Je lui le donne (to say 'I give it to him' instead of 'je le lui donne')
common_error.correct_alt: Je le lui donne (no alternative, but emphasis can be added: 'C'est à lui que je le donne')
common_error.explanation: This error occurs because in Spanish the structure 'se lo' is used, where 'se' is the indirect object pronoun and 'lo' the direct one, but in French the order is always direct + indirect. Spanish speakers tend to transfer the Spanish order, but in French it is reversed: first the direct object (le, la, les) and then the indirect (lui, leur). To avoid this, remember the mnemonic rule: 'direct before indirect' and practice with verbs like 'donner', 'envoyer', 'montrer'.

examples.original: Je te le montre.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə tə lə mɔ̃tʁ/
examples.translation: I show it to you.
examples.note: In French, the indirect object pronoun (te) comes first, then the direct (le), unlike Spanish where 'te lo' is used but can sometimes be confused with 'se lo'.

examples.original: Il nous la raconte.
examples.phonetic: /il nu la ʁakɔ̃t/
examples.translation: He tells it to us.
examples.note: Order: nous (OI) + la (OD) + verb. In Spanish it would be 'nos la cuenta', same order, but be careful with past participle agreement in compound tenses.

examples.original: Tu me les prêtes ?
examples.phonetic: /ty mə le pʁɛt/
examples.translation: Do you lend them to me?
examples.note: Here 'me' is OI and 'les' is OD. In Spanish we say 'me los prestas' with the same order, but in French the past participle will agree if it were in the compound past.

examples.original: Offre-le-moi !
examples.phonetic: /ɔfʁə lə mwa/
examples.translation: Give it to me!
examples.note: In affirmative imperative, pronouns come after the verb joined by hyphens and the order changes: OD + OI, here 'le' (OD) before 'moi' (OI).

examples.original: Expliquez-la-leur !
examples.phonetic: /ɛksplike la lœʁ/
examples.translation: Explain it to them!
examples.note: Here the order is OD (la) + OI (leur). In Spanish it would be 'explíquensela' with a single pronoun, but in French it is broken down.

examples.original: Ne me le dis pas !
examples.phonetic: /nə mə lə di pa/
examples.translation: Don't tell it to me!
examples.note: In negative imperative, pronouns come before the verb as in the indicative, and 'me' precedes 'le' (OI before OD), although in this case 'me' and 'le' are both 1st and 3rd person pronouns, the order follows the same rule.

levels.label: Verbes avec prépositions et pronoms y/en
levels.translation: Verbs with prepositions and pronouns y/en

examples.original: J'y pense souvent.
examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿i pɑ̃s suvɑ̃/
examples.translation: I often think about it.
examples.note: The verb 'penser à' uses the pronoun 'y' which replaces 'à + something'. In Spanish 'pensar en' can use 'ello', but there is no direct equivalent.

examples.original: Il en parle beaucoup.
examples.phonetic: /il ɑ̃ paʁl boku/
examples.translation: He talks a lot about it.
examples.note: The verb 'parler de' uses the pronoun 'en' for 'de + something'. In Spanish, 'hablar de eso' can be said, but the use of 'en' is more specific.

examples.original: Elle s'y est habituée.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl s‿i e ɛ̃te/
examples.translation: She has gotten used to it.
examples.note: Here 'y' replaces 'à + something', and additionally the past participle 'habituée' agrees with the subject because there is no explicit direct object.

examples.original: Nous en avons parlé.
examples.phonetic: /nu z‿ɑ̃ n‿avɔ̃ paʁle/
examples.translation: We have talked about it.
examples.note: With 'en', there is no agreement of the past participle because 'en' is not a specific COD; it is considered an adverbial pronoun. In Spanish, 'hablar de ello'.

title: Nuances entre tiempos y aspectos verbales / Nuances between verb tenses and aspects
bridge: In Spanish, the distinction between the simple past tense and the imperfect tense is fundamental, and in French, something similar happens with the 'passé composé' and the 'imparfait'. However, in French, the 'passé composé' is used for punctual or sequential actions, while the 'imparfait' describes states, habits, or ongoing actions in the past. A typical trap: Spanish speakers often use the 'passé composé' where French prefers the 'imparfait' for background descriptions, and vice versa. Additionally, the 'plus-que-parfait' (equivalent to the pluperfect) and the 'passé simple' (literary) require special attention, as their usage differs from Spanish in terms of register and frequency.
rule: In French, past tenses are distributed according to aspects: the 'imparfait' is used for unbounded actions (habits, descriptions, states), and the 'passé composé' for bounded, punctual, and sequential actions. The 'plus-que-parfait' indicates an action prior to another past action, equivalent to the Spanish pluperfect. The 'passé simple' is the literary narrative tense, used instead of the 'passé composé' in formal written narration, and is uncommon in spoken language. The 'passé antérieur' (very literary) and nuances of the 'futur antérieur' and 'conditionnel passé' for expressing hypotheses should also be considered. For level C1, it is crucial to distinguish between perfective aspect (completed action) and imperfective aspect (ongoing action) in narrative and descriptive contexts, as well as temporal usage in indirect speech.

concept_examples.text: Quand j'étais jeune, je jouais au tennis tous les étés.
concept_examples.translation: When I was young, I used to play tennis every summer.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kɑ̃ ʒ‿etɛ ʒœn | ʒə ʒwɛ o tɛnis tu lez‿ɛte/

concept_examples.text: Hier, j'ai rencontré Marie et nous avons parlé pendant des heures.
concept_examples.translation: Yesterday, I met Marie and we talked for hours.
concept_examples.phonetic: /jɛʁ | ʒ‿e ʁɑ̃kɔ̃tʁe maʁi e nu zavɔ̃ paʁle pɑ̃dɑ̃ dez‿œʁ/

concept_examples.text: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti de la maison.
concept_examples.translation: It was raining when I left the house.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il pløvɛ kɑ̃ ʒə sɥi sɔʁti də la mɛzɔ̃/

concept_examples.text: Elle avait déjà fini son travail quand le chef est arrivé.
concept_examples.translation: She had already finished her work when the boss arrived.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛl avɛ deʒa fini sɔ̃ tʁavaj kɑ̃ lə ʃɛf ɛt‿aʁive/

common_error.wrong: Je suis fatigué parce que je travaillais toute la journée.
common_error.correct: Je suis fatigué parce que j'ai travaillé toute la journée.
common_error.correct_alt: Je suis fatigué parce que j'avais travaillé toute la journée (implies a cause prior to a past moment, less natural here).
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish the imperfect tense 'trabajaba' is used for an action that lasted a period, but in French, when the period is delimited (toute la journée), the aspect is perfective, so the 'passé composé' is used. To describe an ongoing action without delimitation, the 'imparfait' would be used. The key is to distinguish between global aspect (completed action) and developing aspect. In this context, the action of working is completed and bounded, so the 'passé composé' is correct.

examples.original: Quand j'étais enfant, je visitais souvent mes grands-parents.
examples.phonetic: /kɑ̃ ʒ‿etɛ ɑ̃fɑ̃ | ʒə vizitɛ suvɑ̃ me gʁɑ̃ paʁɑ̃/
examples.translation: When I was a child, I often visited my grandparents.
examples.note: The imperfect expresses habitual actions in the past, just like in Spanish.

examples.original: Hier, j'ai visité le musée du Louvre.
examples.phonetic: /jɛʁ | ʒ‿e vizite lə myze dy luvʁ/
examples.translation: Yesterday, I visited the Louvre museum.
examples.note: The 'passé composé' indicates a punctual and completed action, with a time marker.

examples.original: Comme il faisait beau, nous avons décidé de marcher.
examples.phonetic: /kɔm il fəzɛ bo | nu zavɔ̃ deside də maʁʃe/
examples.translation: Since the weather was nice, we decided to walk.
examples.note: The imperfect sets the context (description) and the 'passé composé' the main action.

examples.original: J'avais déjà mangé quand ils sont arrivés.
examples.phonetic: /ʒ‿avɛ deʒa mɑ̃ʒe kɑ̃ il sɔ̃t‿aʁive/
examples.translation: I had already eaten when they arrived.
examples.note: The 'plus-que-parfait' expresses anteriority with respect to the 'passé composé', just like in Spanish.

examples.original: Elle n'a pas pu venir parce qu'elle avait perdu la clé.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl n‿a pa py vəniʁ paʁsk‿ɛl avɛ pɛʁdy la kle/
examples.translation: She couldn't come because she had lost the key.
examples.note: The action of losing is prior to the action of not being able to come; the 'plus-que-parfait' clarifies this.

examples.original: Quand je suis arrivé, le film avait déjà commencé.
examples.phonetic: /kɑ̃ ʒə sɥi zaʁive | lə film avɛ deʒa kɔmɑ̃se/
examples.translation: When I arrived, the movie had already started.
examples.note: The 'plus-que-parfait' places the action of starting before the arrival, which is in 'passé composé'.

levels.label: Passé simple et récit littéraire
levels.translation: Simple past tense and literary narration

examples.original: Il prit la lettre et la déchira sans un mot.
examples.phonetic: /il pʁi la lɛtʁ e la deʃiʁa sɑ̃z‿œ̃ mo/
examples.translation: He took the letter and tore it up without a word.
examples.note: In literature, the 'passé simple' (simple past tense) is used for sequential actions; it is not used in speech. Note the third person: prit and déchira.

examples.original: Tout à coup, le ciel s'obscurcit et un vent violent se leva.
examples.phonetic: /tu ta ku | lə sjɛl s‿ɔpskyʁsi e œ̃ vɑ̃ vjɔlɑ̃ sə ləva/
examples.translation: Suddenly, the sky darkened and a violent wind rose.
examples.note: The 'passé simple' describes punctual events in a narrative, similar to the Spanish simple past tense, but only in formal/literary register.

examples.original: Pendant ce temps, les habitants de la ville dormaient paisiblement.
examples.phonetic: /pɑ̃dɑ̃ sə tɑ̃ | lez‿abitɑ̃ də la vil dɔʁmɛ pɛzibləmɑ̃/
examples.translation: Meanwhile, the inhabitants of the city were sleeping peacefully.
examples.note: In narration, the 'imparfait' is used for background description, while the 'passé simple' is used for main events.

translations.en: Nuances between verb tenses and aspects

title: Les passives avancées / Advanced passives
bridge: In Spanish, we use impersonal structures with 'se' or constructions like 'se cree que' to express opinions or rumors. In French, these are formed with 'il est + participe passé' or 'on dit que'. The big difference: French uses the impersonal pronoun 'il' and requires agreement of the past participle with the grammatical subject, something that does not exist in Spanish. Be careful with the use of 'il est' + adjective vs. 'il est' + participe passé to avoid confusing the passive voice with the attributive one.
rule: Advanced passives in French express opinion, belief or rumor. They are mainly formed with: (1) 'il est + participe passé + que' (e.g. il est dit que), (2) 'il est + adjective + de + infinitive' (e.g. il est difficile de), (3) impersonal 'on' (e.g. on dit que), and (4) passive with verbs of opinion in impersonal form (e.g. il est considéré comme). The participle must agree in gender and number with the logical subject when it appears (e.g. 'elles sont dites intelligentes'). In sentences with 'que', the subjunctive is used if the main verb expresses doubt, but with verbs of certainty the indicative is used. With 'on', the verb is always in the third person singular. Avoid translating 'se cree' literally as 'se croit'; it should be 'on croit' or 'il est cru que'.

concept_examples.text: Il est dit que le président va démissionner.
concept_examples.translation: Se dice que el presidente va a dimitir.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il‿e di kə lə pʁe.zi.dɑ̃ va de.mi.sjɔ.ne/

concept_examples.text: On considère que cette décision est importante.
concept_examples.translation: Se considera que esta decisión es importante.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ kɔ̃.si.dɛʁ kə sɛt de.si.zjɔ̃ ɛt‿ɛ̃.pɔʁ.tɑ̃t/

concept_examples.text: Il est difficile de comprendre cette théorie.
concept_examples.translation: Es difícil de entender esta teoría.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il‿e di.fi.sil də kɔ̃.pʁɑ̃dʁ sɛt te.ɔ.ʁi/

concept_examples.text: Les résultats sont dits satisfaisants.
concept_examples.translation: Los resultados se dicen satisfactorios.
concept_examples.phonetic: /le ʁe.zyl.ta sɔ̃ di sa.tis.fə.zɑ̃/

common_error.wrong: Se croit que le changement est nécessaire.
common_error.correct: On croit que le changement est nécessaire.
common_error.correct_alt: Il est cru que le changement est nécessaire.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'se cree' is formed with the pronoun 'se'. In French, there is no direct equivalent; you must use 'on' (which means 'one, people') or the impersonal construction 'il est + participe passé'. Using 'se croit' is a direct calque from Spanish and is incorrect. Remember that 'on' is the most common and natural form in French to express impersonal statements.

examples.original: Il est annoncé que les prix vont augmenter.
examples.phonetic: /il‿e.t‿a.nɔ̃.se kə le pʁi vɔ̃ oɡ.mɑ̃.te/
examples.translation: Se anuncia que los precios van a subir.
examples.note: Use of 'il est + participe passé' for rumors or announcements.

examples.original: Il est estimé que plus de mille personnes ont participé.
examples.phonetic: /il‿e.t‿ɛs.ti.me kə ply də mil pɛʁ.sɔn ɔ̃ paʁ.ti.si.pe/
examples.translation: Se estima que más de mil personas participaron.
examples.note: The participle 'estimé' agrees with 'il' (masculine singular).

examples.original: Il est supposé que le projet sera terminé en juin.
examples.phonetic: /il‿e sy.po.ze kə lə pʁɔ.ʒɛ sə.ʁa tɛʁ.mi.ne ɑ̃ ʒɥɛ̃/
examples.translation: Se supone que el proyecto estará terminado en junio.
examples.note: With verbs of supposition, the indicative or subjunctive is used depending on the context.

examples.original: On dit que la mer est belle aujourd'hui.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ di kə la mɛʁ e bɛl o.ʒuʁ.dɥi/
examples.translation: Se dice que el mar está hermoso hoy.
examples.note: Use of 'on' as an indefinite subject to express general opinion.

examples.original: On croit que les extraterrestres existent.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ kʁwa kə le ɛk.stʁa.tɛ.ʁɛs.tʁ‿ɛɡ.zist/
examples.translation: Se cree que los extraterrestres existen.
examples.note: The verb 'croire' followed by 'que' and the indicative because it expresses belief.

examples.original: On raconte que ce château est hanté.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ ʁa.kɔ̃t kə sə ʃa.to e ɑ̃.te/
examples.translation: Se cuenta que este castillo está encantado.
examples.note: Use of 'on raconte' to narrate legends or stories.

examples.original: On prétend qu'il a gagné le prix.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ pʁe.tɑ̃ kil‿a ɡa.ɲe lə pʁi/
examples.translation: Se pretende que él ganó el premio.
examples.note: In French, 'prétendre' can mean to claim without certainty.

levels.label: Passive avec verbes de perception et d'opinion
levels.translation: Passive with verbs of perception and opinion

examples.original: Cette théorie est considérée comme complexe.
examples.phonetic: /sɛt te.ɔ.ʁi e kɔ̃.si.de.ʁe kɔm kɔ̃.plɛks/
examples.translation: Esta teoría es considerada como compleja.
examples.note: Use of 'être considéré comme' + adjective; the participle agrees with the subject.

examples.original: Les résultats sont jugés insuffisants.
examples.phonetic: /le ʁe.zyl.ta sɔ̃ ʒy.ʒe ɛ̃.sy.fi.zɑ̃/
examples.translation: Los resultados son juzgados como insuficientes.
examples.note: The participle 'jugés' agrees with 'résultats' (masculine plural).

examples.original: Elle est reconnue comme une experte.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl e ʁə.kɔ.ny kɔm yn ɛk.spɛʁt/
examples.translation: Ella es reconocida como experta.
examples.note: Agreement of the participle with feminine subject: 'reconnue'.

examples.original: On a été surpris de l'annonce.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ a e.te syʁ.pʁi də la.nɔ̃s/
examples.translation: Nos sorprendió el anuncio.
examples.note: Note: this structure with 'être surpris de' is equivalent to 'sorprenderse de' in Spanish.
